source: written from the sources only, by an agent that never saw a page

questions.question: What is the fish parable meant to show, and why does Wallace insist he is not the 'wise old fish'?
questions.reference: The parable shows that the most obvious, important realities are the hardest to see and talk about, because we are immersed in them. Wallace disowns the role of wise old fish because he is not claiming superior insight; he admits the point sounds like a banal platitude, but argues that in daily adult life such platitudes can matter enormously.
key_points: The most obvious, important realities are the hardest to see/talk about (we are immersed in them like water)
Wallace does not claim to be wiser than the audience; he says the platitude can still be of life-or-death importance in daily adult life

questions.question: According to Wallace, what does the cliché 'a liberal arts education teaches you how to think' really mean, and why is it not insulting?
questions.reference: It is not about the capacity to think, which graduates already have, but about the choice of what to think about. More deeply, it means exercising some control over how and what you think: being aware enough to choose what you pay attention to and how you construct meaning from experience. Without that, the mind becomes 'a terrible master'.
key_points: Not about the ability/capacity to think but the choice of what to think about
Choosing what to pay attention to and how to construct meaning from experience
Otherwise you are a slave to your head (mind as excellent servant, terrible master)

questions.question: What is the 'default setting', and why does Wallace say that changing it is not a matter of virtue?
questions.reference: The default setting is our hard-wired, natural self-centeredness: since we are the center of every experience we have, we automatically believe we are the center of the universe and interpret everything through the lens of self. Adjusting it is not about being morally good or compassionate as a virtue; it is a matter of choosing to do the work of altering or getting free of that automatic setting, i.e. being 'well-adjusted'.
key_points: Default setting = hard-wired, automatic self-centeredness (everything experienced as about me, since I'm at the center of every experience)
It is shared by everyone and comes from how experience works, not from bad character
Changing it is chosen work/effort of awareness (being 'well-adjusted'), not moral virtue or being a good person

questions.question: What does Wallace use the story of the atheist and the religious man in the Alaskan bar to show? What is his point about arrogance and certainty?
questions.reference: The standard reading is that the same experience can mean different things to different people, but Wallace pushes further: how we construct meaning is a personal, intentional choice, not something hard-wired or simply absorbed. He also faults the atheist's total certainty that the Eskimos had nothing to do with his prayer, and says religious dogmatists share the same problem; blind certainty is a prison so total the prisoner doesn't know he's locked up. Learning to think means being a little less arrogant and more critically aware of one's own certainties.
key_points: The same experience can be given different meanings; how we construct meaning is a matter of choice, not hard-wired
The problem is blind certainty/arrogance (the atheist's, and equally religious dogmatists'), not which side is right
Learning to think = being a little less arrogant, with critical awareness of one's own certainties, many of which are wrong

questions.question: In the supermarket and traffic example, what exactly is the choice Wallace describes, and why does he place it in such boring, petty moments?
questions.reference: On the default setting, the tired shopper experiences the crowd, lines and traffic as all about MY hunger and fatigue, with everyone else in the way (even the 'socially conscious' version, disgust at SUV drivers, is still default). The choice is to consciously consider other possibilities, e.g. that others are just as tired or have harder lives, or that the Hummer driver is rushing a sick child to hospital. Petty routine is where adult life is mostly lived, so that is exactly where the work of choosing comes in.
key_points: Default reaction: the situation is all about me and others are in my way (including the self-righteous 'socially conscious' version)
The choice is what to pay attention to and how to interpret others, e.g. imagining their harder circumstances
Everyday boredom/routine/frustration is where adult life happens, so that is where the choice matters

questions.question: What does Wallace mean by 'everybody worships', and what happens to people who worship money, their body/beauty, power or intellect? What makes these forms of worship insidious?
questions.reference: There is no such thing as not worshipping; the only choice is what to worship, and almost anything other than something spiritual or an inviolable set of ethical principles 'will eat you alive'. Worship money and you never have enough; body and beauty, you always feel ugly; power, you feel weak and afraid and need more; intellect, you feel stupid, a fraud about to be found out. The insidious part is not that they are evil or sinful but that they are unconscious default settings you slip into gradually.
key_points: Everyone worships something; the only choice is what
Each object of worship produces its own lack: never enough money, always ugly, weak and afraid, a fraud
The danger is that such worship is unconscious/a default setting you slip into, not that it's sinful

questions.question: Applied: A coworker sends you a curt, one-line reply to a long email you worked hard on, and you feel insulted. Describe what Wallace's default setting would do here and what his alternative would look like. Would he say you are obliged to respond the second way?
questions.reference: The default setting would read the reply as being about me: disrespect, rudeness, an injustice to my effort, with total certainty about what it means. Wallace's alternative is to notice that reaction and consciously consider other possibilities, e.g. the coworker is overwhelmed, dealing with a crisis, or just writes tersely; these may not be likely, but they are not impossible. He would not say you are morally obliged: it is hard, takes will and effort, some days you won't manage, and it's about choosing your attention, not being virtuous.
key_points: Default: automatically interpret it as about me / a slight, with certainty
Alternative: be aware and deliberately consider other plausible explanations for the other person's behaviour
Not a moral rule: it's a choice that takes effort and sometimes fails, not about being virtuous or right

questions.question: Applied: A successful friend says, 'I'm totally free: I earn well, I answer to no one, and I can do whatever I want.' How would Wallace distinguish that freedom from 'real freedom', and what might he warn about?
questions.reference: Wallace would grant that this kind of freedom, to be 'lords of our tiny skull-sized kingdoms, alone at the centre of all creation', has much to recommend it, but it is the freedom the culture of money and power promotes and it fits the default setting. Real freedom involves attention, awareness and discipline, and truly caring about and sacrificing for other people in petty, unsexy ways every day. He might warn that if money or status is what the friend worships, they will never feel they have enough, and the alternative is the rat race and 'the constant gnawing sense of having had, and lost, some infinite thing.'
key_points: The friend's freedom is the self-centred 'lord of a skull-sized kingdom' kind the culture rewards; Wallace grants it has merits but calls it the lesser kind
Real freedom = attention, awareness, discipline, and caring for/sacrificing for others in small daily ways
Warning: worshipping money/status is unconscious default and never satisfies (never enough; rat race, gnawing loss)
